rows.description: A toddler notices whether a parent is crouched down and relaxed or standing stiff. A lowered, open posture usually feels safe, while looming and tense feels threatening; young children react to the body long before understanding the words.

rows.subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
rows.description: A schoolchild learns that teachers read upright sitting as attention and slouching as boredom. Slouching may instead mean tiredness, low mood or a comfortable way of thinking, so posture is a clue, not proof of attitude.

A student reads a friend leaning forward as interest and leaning back as relaxed or distant. These are weak cues; a person leaning back may be comfortable, or unwell, so checking with a question is wiser than concluding disinterest.
A student spreads study across days, recalls answers without looking, and revisits material just as it begins to fade. It feels harder and works better.
A working adult keeps notes, reviews key skills at intervals, and treats forgetting as the mind's ordinary filtering rather than a sign of failing.
A child blinks, sniffs or makes sounds they cannot fully control, with urges that build before them. Tics often rise with stress and excitement and fall when absorbed, and shame makes them worse.
A teenager may suppress tics at school then release them at home, feeling tired and self-conscious. Not blamed or told to stop, they cope better; a doctor can explain options if tics cause trouble.

rows.subtype: Child freezes and cries at a friend's fall [Actor]
rows.description: A child sees a friend fall, cries loudly and cannot move; their own distress swamps them, so no help comes, though the caring feeling is real.

rows.subtype: Overwhelmed by a friend's crisis, then withdrawing [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager absorbs a friend's grief, sleeps badly, and starts avoiding the friend out of exhaustion; too much feeling-with can end in pulling away from the one who needs them.

rows.subtype: Caring role wears the carer down [Actor]
rows.description: A nursing or counselling student feels every patient's pain, grows numb and irritable, and wonders if they care less; this is fatigue from over-feeling, not a lack of heart.
A child who fears being wrong will only do puzzles they already know how to solve; avoiding failure feels safe but also blocks learning.
A teenager who lost a debate feels their worth has dropped and avoids the next contest; fear is about what failing says about them and not about the task.
A student picks the easy course to protect a high grade point average and never tries the field they love; fear of falling short quietly makes the choices.

rows.subtype: Different ways of relating in toddlerhood [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler may prefer lining up objects, respond less to their name or become very upset by changed routine, and show love in their own ways. Behaviour is what is described here, and a paediatrician can assess concerns.
A teenager copies peers' expressions and scripts to fit in, then melts down or shuts down at home. Hiding natural ways takes great energy, and acceptance at home offers a place to rest.

An autistic adult may find open-plan offices, small talk and unclear expectations draining but thrive with clear tasks and written instructions. Asking for adjustments is reasonable, and being understood is a relief.
